edges.description: SPEN is a transcriptional repressor, so halving its dose reduces the repressive activity it recruits to target genes.

The X-silencing function of SPEN was established by complete loss of SPEN in mouse cells and embryos. Whether a single remaining SPEN copy is enough for normal X inactivation in human females has not been tested; the female X-chromosome methylation episignature is the only human observation pointing that way.
SPEN is needed for several developmental processes, but the de-repressed genes and the neural cell types that carry the defect in patients are not identified.

In the mouse, Spen loss reduces palatal mesenchyme proliferation and delays shelf elevation; Spen interacts genetically with the RERE co-repressor in this process. The transcriptional targets involved are not identified.

In Drosophila, Spen acts cell-autonomously in fat-storage cells to permit lipid mobilization, and mouse Spen transcript levels track body fat. This is a candidate explanation for the obesity in RATARS, not a demonstrated human mechanism.

nodes.description: XIST RNA recruits SPEN to the future inactive X through SPEN RRM4 and the XIST A-repeat; SPEN then recruits SMRT/HDAC3, histones are deacetylated and RNA polymerase II is excluded, initiating silencing. In mouse, SPEN is essential to initiate X inactivation but dispensable for its maintenance in neural progenitors, where it still dampens expression of escape genes. All of this comes from complete loss of SPEN; the effect of heterozygous loss on human X inactivation is untested.

nodes.description: SPEN (also called SHARP or MINT) binds RNA through its RRM domains and, via its C-terminal SPOC domain, recruits the NCoR/SMRT co-repressor and HDAC3 as well as NuRD, m6A and RNA polymerase II machinery. In mouse it also competes with the Notch intracellular domain for RBP-J and so dampens Notch-dependent transactivation. Which developmental target genes are de-repressed in RATARS patients is unknown.
